PART 4 — Why Loving People Turn Controlling

4.1 The Fear–Control Loop

4.2 Ten Reasons Ordinary People Slide Into It

  1. Anxiety that has no other outlet. A threatened sense of safety pushes toward whatever relieves anxiety fastest, and control often does so in the short term. (Neuroscience generally describes threat responses and their relief as reinforcing, which is why the pattern strengthens; it is a common simplification, not a mechanism specific to controlling parents.)
  2. Identity invested in the other. "A good mother is one whose children turn out well." If the child's choices measure the parent, every choice feels like a verdict.
  3. Shame and image. In honour–shame settings the family's reputation can feel at stake. The child becomes a carrier of the family's face.
  4. An unlived life. A parent who was denied choices may either insist on the same sacrifices ("I managed, so can you") or live through the child's achievements.
  5. Own history repeated. Someone who was controlled, or neglected, can reproduce control or over-compensate with it.
  6. Love learned as management. Some people only saw love shown as worrying, rules and sacrifice, and do not know another way.
  7. Fear of loss of role. As children grow, a parent's job changes; some cannot bear being less needed.
  8. Fusion. When people's selves are not separate (enmeshment), someone else's difference feels like loss or attack.
  9. The system rewards it. Compliance is praised; refusal is punished by relatives and community, so the controller is pushed by others as well.
  10. Good intentions as cover. "I only want what's best" lets a person avoid asking whose need is actually being met. The earlier study on justification applies here.

4.3 The Slide: From Care to Control

Few people begin at the far end. Each step can feel like love from the inside, which is why it is easy to miss.

4.4 Does This Make Them a "Monster"?

People are not monsters, but impact is real whatever the intent. Two things are true together:

  • Most controlling "love" is fear-driven and unaware. The person genuinely believes they are loving. Naming the underlying fear is the way into change.
  • Some control is not just fear but entitlement: a belief that another person exists to serve, obey or reflect me. When it includes monitoring, isolating, intimidation, financial control or violence (coercive control), more than "unmet needs" is going on. It is a pattern of power, it needs boundaries, accountability and often outside protection, and the relational gospel does not ask the person harmed to absorb it quietly (see Part 8).

PART 5 — How God Loves: Love That Does Not Coerce

The relational gospel (the framework of this series, drawing on Kruger and others; paraphrased, not quoted) reads God's love as real, persistent and non-coercive: the Triune God has included us in His life and will not stop loving, yet does not override a person's will or manipulate. If God does not control those He loves, controlling love is not a picture of God's love. Scripture shows this pattern repeatedly.

5.1 What the Scripture Shows

PassageWhat happensWhat it shows about love
Luke 15:11-24 — the prodigal and his fatherThe father divides the property when asked (v12), lets the son go, then watches the road: "while he was still a long way off, his father saw him" (v20)Love allows a foolish choice, does not stop loving, and runs to welcome. It neither blocks nor abandons.
Mark 10:17-22 — the rich young ruler"Jesus, looking at him, loved him (egapesen)" and told him the truth. The man walked away sad. Jesus does not chase with threats or tricks.Love speaks truth clearly and lets the person decide.
Matt 23:37 — over Jerusalem"How often would I have gathered your children… and you were not willing (ouk ethelesate)."God's desire does not override human will; grief remains the cost of love.
Rev 3:20"I stand at the door and knock."Persistent invitation, no forced entry.
Philemon 8-9, 14Paul says he could command, but appeals (parakaleo) in love and will do nothing without consent, so that the good would be "not by compulsion (kata anagken) but of your own accord (kata hekousion)."Even when a leader has authority, love seeks free consent.
2 Cor 1:24; 1 Pet 5:3; Matt 20:25-28"Not that we lord it over (kyrieuomen) your faith"; elders are not to be "domineering" (katakyrieuontes); rulers "lord it over" but "it shall not be so among you."Leadership in the kingdom is service, not domination.
Matt 16:21-23 — PeterPeter, out of apparent love, rebukes Jesus for planning to suffer: "Far be it from you!" Jesus says "get behind me… you are a stumbling block (skandalon)."Even well-meant protection can block someone's calling; "caring" can oppose what God is doing in a person.
Mark 3:21Jesus' family "went out to seize him (kratesai), for they were saying, 'He is out of his mind.'"Families can sincerely try to restrain a loved one, wrongly.

Where Christians disagree. (1) Authority and submission. Some traditions give husbands or church leaders strong decision-making authority; others read Eph 5:21 ("submitting to one another") as mutual. Nearly all agree that Scripture's authority language does not license coercion, intimidation or abuse. (2) "Compel them to come in" (Luke 14:23, anagkason) has been used to justify force; many read it as an urgent, persistent invitation within a parable about a banquet, not a command to coerce a person's conscience. (3) Parents of adults. Traditions differ on how long "obey" (Eph 6:1, addressed to children) applies, and on how far "honour" extends into adult decisions. The general view is that obedience is for children in the household, and honour continues for life as respect, not submission.

PART 6 — "Do We Just Watch Them Spoil?" The Third Way

The question assumes only two choices: force them or stand by. The relational gospel offers a third: stay, tell the truth, offer help, let consequences teach, protect the vulnerable, and keep the door open. That is neither passive nor controlling.

6.1 Three Circles: What I Control, Influence, and Must Entrust

6.2 The Ladder of Legitimate Influence

Before force, there are many honest, non-coercive steps. Each is love in action, and each leaves the other free.

#StepWhat it looks likeWhat to avoid
1Settle my own fear firstName the fear and bring it to the Father before speaking; ask "what is mine here?"Speaking from panic
2Listen to understandAsk what they are thinking, wanting and afraid of; reflect it back accuratelyListening only to rebut
3Ask permission"Would you like to hear my concern? You can say no."Ambushing with a group
4Say it once, clearly"I'm afraid that… because… I may be wrong. Whatever you decide, I'm with you."Repeating daily, guilt, "I told you so"
5Offer help and informationResources, introductions, a counsellor, a trial period, a plan B they can chooseHiding information; making help conditional
6Set my own limits"I won't fund this. I won't lie for you. I'm glad to see you whenever you want."Limits designed to punish or force
7Allow natural consequencesDon't rescue or erase the results of their choice; stay warm while they face themRescuing, then resenting
8Protect those who can't protect themselvesChildren, the elderly with dementia, someone in immediate danger (Part 8)Using "protection" for preferences
9Pray, keep the door open, watch the roadRemain reachable; be ready to welcome without "I told you so" (Luke 15:20)Cutting off; waiting for an apology first

A word on grief. Watching someone choose a path you believe will harm them is painful, and that pain is part of love, not a sign of failure. The Father's own grief (Matt 23:37) shows it. The answer to the grief is not control. It is being carried in it, and not carrying alone what belongs to Him.
